newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: EMU raises volume on futures open outcry debate.
newsitem.headline: EMU raises volume on futures open outcry debate.

text.p: Futures executives at a conference here were divided on what changes European Monetary Union (EMU) will bring to the industry, as well as what type of exchange will best survive in the new European environment.

London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE) officials say they have the best of both worlds, with an electronic after-hours "APT" or automated pit trading system augmenting floor trade.

"Basically, it is an issue about screen-based (systems) or traditional open outcry plus screen-based, which we are. We're much higher-tech than any (other) exchange," Jack Wigglesworth, LIFFE chairman, told reporters.
But Deutsche Boerse executives scoff at suggestions open-outcry will survive much beyond this century.
"Look to the past move from sailing ships to steamers, the move from horses to cars," said Joerg Franke, a senior Deutsche Boerse executive.

Deutsche Boerse is the operating company for Germany's main stock exchange and its futures and options exchange Deutsche Terminboerse (DTB), which is fully electronic. Bourse officials say DTB has proved it can master huge volume on an electronic exchange.
"When we started ... nobody wanted to believe that such a big volume could be traded on an electronic exchange. But we have traded 630,000 contracts a day without any problem," Franke said.
LIFFE officials say electronic trade may one day dominate, but it would take more than computer networks. They believe it will require simulated pits and a virtual floor.
Chicago's huge futures exchanges, the Chicago Mercantile Exchange and the Chicago Board of Trade, both rely on traditional open-outcry.
But even Chicago exchanges are using electronic systems for after-hours trading. And most of the newer futures exchanges are electronic.

Stock exchanges throughout Europe are already mostly electronic. The Frankfurt stock exchange plans to shift cash trade to a new electronic order matching system in 1998. Swiss stock exchanges just moved domestic shares and bonds to an electronic system in August.

"The move toward more automation is very clear," said U.S. fund manager Mark Boucher, president of Investment Research Associates. But he said this may be more the case with stocks than futures. "Elements of human interaction are critical to price discovery" with respect to futures, he said.

EMU, which foresees a single European "euro" currency being phased in starting in 1999, and the rise of the Internet are making geographic boundaries less important. This should, in theory, create closer electronic ties among European exchanges.

But DTB and France's Matif have just terminated a planned cooperation that would have created a joint electronic trading platform for listed derivatives. Matif may look to another link-up, possibly with a U.S. exchange.
Franke noted such a link with DTB was only possible electronically. But he says "Our French friends believe electronic and floor trade is the right solution."
DTB meanwhile is opening the way for its members to trade directly from remote sites in Chicago. It expects to have six such sites by the end of the year.

LIFFE officials note, however, that DTB's terminals at member firms in London have thus far failed to give it an edge in trading Deutschmark products. They say LIFFE still has more than 95 percent of the short-term Deutschemark futures market.
"At the end of the day, it is the markets which will decide. The markets are currently saying the old order will become the new order," said Daniel Hodson, chief executive of LIFFE.
Franke is not likely to be convinced so easily. "Anywhere in the next century it will happen. Even Chicago and New York will trade electronically," he said. -- Zurich Editorial, +41 1 631 7340
